client: I've been feeling really overwhelmed lately because my thesis deadlines are creeping up on me, and I just can't seem to get on top of everything. On top of that, I'm still working my part-time job and trying to keep up with friends, and it all feels like too much at once. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to help, because at the end of the day the deadlines are still going to be there no matter what we discuss.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a really heavy load right now — the pressure of your thesis, work, and friendships all pressing down at once — and even though your words are rushing out, there's something in your voice that sounds quietly exhausted beneath all of that. You're right that talking won't make the deadlines disappear, but what we *can* do together is help you find a way to think about all of this that feels less like everything is crashing in at once. Sometimes when we're overwhelmed, our mind treats every task as equally urgent and equally impossible — and gently untangling that can make a real difference in what feels manageable.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: Yeah, exhausted is definitely the right word — I don't think I've had a full night's sleep in weeks because my brain just won't shut off about everything I haven't done yet. I hear what you're saying about untangling things, but honestly when I try to sit down and prioritize, it still feels like every single thing is urgent and I end up just freezing instead of doing anything. I guess I'm not sure how thinking about it differently actually translates into getting the work done.
therapist: The way you're speaking — fast, loud, with a real edge of urgency — tells me your nervous system is genuinely activated right now, even as your words are trying to stay rational and questioning, and that gap between the two makes a lot of sense when you haven't slept properly in weeks. That freezing you're describing isn't laziness or weakness — it's actually a very predictable response when your brain perceives *everything* as a threat at once, like a fire alarm going off in every room simultaneously. In CBT terms, we'd want to gently challenge the thought that "everything is equally urgent right now," because that belief itself is likely what's keeping you stuck — and finding even one small, concrete action to take can start to break that freeze response.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: I actually hadn't thought about it as a fire alarm going off everywhere at once, and that does kind of describe it — like there's no way to know which one to run to first. But I'm skeptical about the "one small action" thing, because I've read about that kind of advice before and when I try it, I just end up feeling guilty that I'm only doing something small when the whole thesis is looming over me. It's like no matter what I do, it doesn't feel like enough.
therapist: The way you're speaking right now — fast, loud, with a real intensity — tells me this guilt you're describing isn't just a passing thought, it's something that hits hard and feels very real in your body. What you've just identified is actually a really important pattern: your mind has set up a rule where *small* automatically equals *not enough*, which means no action you take can ever feel like a win — and that rule is worth examining, because it's likely doing more to keep you stuck than the thesis itself is. Where do you think that standard of "it has to be big or it doesn't count" comes from, and is there any evidence that smaller, consistent steps have actually moved things forward for you in the past?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client: I think that standard probably comes from my family — like, growing up, doing well was just expected, and anything less than excellent felt like a failure, so I internalized that pretty deeply. And yeah, if I'm being honest, there have been times where just writing a paragraph a day actually did add up over a few weeks, but in the moment it never felt like progress, it just felt like falling behind. So even when smaller steps technically work, my brain doesn't register them as wins, which makes it really hard to keep going with that approach.
therapist: There's something really significant in what you just shared — your voice is moving quickly, almost like you're rushing through something that actually deserves to slow down and be acknowledged, because you've just made a genuinely important connection between your family's expectations and the impossible standard your brain holds you to today. You also gave yourself some real evidence just now: paragraph by paragraph *did* add up, which means the strategy works — the problem isn't the approach, it's that your mind has been trained to filter out proof of progress and only register what's still undone. That filter was probably a useful survival tool growing up, but right now it's working against you, and noticing it — like you just did — is actually the first step toward loosening its grip.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: It's kind of uncomfortable to hear it framed that way, because it makes me realize how long I've been running on this setting without even questioning it. But I'm not sure "noticing it" is enough — like, okay, I can see the filter is there, but when I'm sitting at my desk at midnight panicking about my thesis, how does that awareness actually stop the panic in that moment? It feels like there's still a big gap between understanding something intellectually and it actually changing how I feel.
therapist: The way you're speaking — your voice pitched high and moving quickly even as the words themselves stay measured — tells me this question is coming from a genuinely urgent place, not just intellectual curiosity, and that gap you're describing between understanding and feeling is one of the most honest things a person can name in therapy. You're absolutely right that insight alone doesn't stop a midnight panic, and CBT doesn't actually ask it to — what it does offer are concrete in-the-moment tools, like grounding techniques or a specific thought to practice *before* you're at that desk at midnight, so your brain has something to reach for when the panic hits. The awareness we've built today is the foundation, but next we can work on building you something more practical to hold onto in those moments — would that feel like a useful direction to take this?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Yeah, I think that does feel like a useful direction, though I'll be honest — I've tried breathing exercises before and they never really worked for me in the middle of a panic, it just felt silly and didn't actually calm me down. So I guess I'm open to hearing what you have in mind, but I'm a bit worried it's going to be something that sounds good in theory but falls apart when I'm actually sitting there at midnight with my thesis open and nothing written. What kind of thing are you thinking?
therapist: Your voice is soft but moving quickly, and there's something in that combination that feels like cautious hope trying to stay protected from disappointment — and that's completely fair given that you've already tried things that didn't land. Breathing exercises aren't the right fit for everyone, and I'd actually want to work *with* your skepticism rather than around it, because what tends to work at midnight isn't a technique that feels foreign, but something that directly interrupts the specific thought pattern keeping you frozen — like having a prepared, honest response ready for when your brain says "nothing I do is enough." What if we worked together right now to build something that's tailored to *your* version of that midnight panic, rather than a generic tool?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: That actually sounds more appealing than I expected, because at least it's not just handing me a one-size-fits-all technique and hoping it sticks. I guess my worry is that whatever we come up with here, in this room where I'm relatively calm, is going to feel hollow or fake when I'm actually in that panicked state and my brain is telling me everything is falling apart. But I'm willing to try — so where do we even start with something like that?
therapist: Your voice has a kind of stretched, effortful quality right now — like you're reaching toward something hopeful while bracing for it not to work — and that tension actually tells us something really useful about where to start. The reason things can feel hollow in a panic is that our brain needs to have *rehearsed* the response enough times in calm moments that it becomes almost automatic, so we'd begin by identifying the exact thought that hits hardest at midnight — something like "I'm failing and it's too late" — and then crafting a specific, honest counter that *you* actually believe, not something that sounds like a poster on a wall. So let's start there: what's the one thought that tends to show up first when the panic kicks in at your desk?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I think the first thought that hits is something like "you've wasted so much time already that there's no way to catch up now," and it comes with this sinking feeling in my chest like the ground is dropping out. It's almost like my brain does a quick calculation and decides the deficit is too large to recover from, so why even bother starting. And the tricky part is that in that moment, it doesn't feel like a distortion — it feels completely factual and obvious.
therapist: The way you described that — "the ground dropping out" — and the heaviness I can hear in your voice even as you're speaking carefully and clearly, tells me this thought carries a real physical weight, not just a mental one, and that makes complete sense given how deeply it's wired in. Here's what's worth holding onto though: that thought presents itself as a calculation, as *fact*, but it's actually a prediction — and your brain has been wrong about this before, because you just told me earlier that paragraph-by-paragraph *did* add up, which means the deficit was never as unrecoverable as it felt. So the counter we build might sound something like: "my brain is doing the calculation again, but it has a proven track record of getting this wrong" — does that feel like something you could actually believe, even a little?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: Honestly, that framing does land a bit differently than I expected — like, framing it as a prediction with a bad track record rather than a fact feels slightly less impossible to argue with. But I think my worry is that in the moment, my brain is going to say "no, this time it's different, this time the deficit really is too big," and then the counter just collapses. How do I stop myself from just talking myself back out of it when the panic takes over?
therapist: The urgency in your voice right now — high, fast, loud — tells me this isn't a hypothetical worry, it's something your brain is already doing *right now* in anticipation, which actually proves how strong that pattern is and why it deserves a real answer. The key is to build the counter so that it already includes that objection — so instead of leaving a gap for your brain to say "but this time is different," the full response becomes something like: "my brain is telling me this time is different, and it has said that every single time before, and it has been wrong every single time before." We're essentially writing the script one step ahead of the panic, so there's no opening left for it to sneak back in — does it feel like that version closes the gap a little more?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: That version does feel more complete, like it's actually anticipating the loophole my brain would find instead of leaving it open. I think I could almost believe it — or at least not immediately dismiss it — which is more than I can say for most things I've tried. My one remaining worry is whether I'll actually remember to use it in the moment, because when the panic hits I kind of lose access to anything I've prepared and it all just goes blank.
therapist: Your voice has settled into something quieter and more measured than earlier in our conversation, which tells me you're genuinely engaging with this rather than just going through the motions — and that "almost believe it" is actually a meaningful shift worth recognizing. The blanking you're describing during panic is real and common, which is exactly why we'd want to make this physical and external rather than something you have to retrieve from memory — something as simple as a sticky note on your laptop with just that one sentence, so your eyes land on it before your brain has a chance to go blank. That way you're not relying on memory under pressure, you're just reading something you already agreed with when you were calm.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech
